en: The Philippine eagle, our national bird, features a shaggy dark brown crest and uses its sharp talons to hunt monkeys and large birds.
Our national flower, the sampaguita, blooms with fragrant white petals that open at night and close during the heat of the day.
The narra tree, the national tree, produces hard, reddish brown wood and has compound leaves that fold together when touched or during heavy rain.
The Ifugao built stone-walled rice terraces using a complex gravity-fed irrigation system that channels mountain spring water down through the cascading paddies without pumps.
During the Lucban Pahiyas festival, locals decorate houses with kiping, which are leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice and natural plant dyes that dry into flexible sheets.
National Scientist Angel Alcala pioneered the establishment of coral reef sanctuaries in the Philippines to protect marine biodiversity and restore local fish populations.
While exiled in Dapitan, national hero Jose Rizal collected over 300 species of local plants, shells, and insects to study and send abroad.
The Philippine tarsier, found in Bohol, has enormous eyes that are actually larger than its brain, allowing it to see clearly in darkness.
The carabao, our national animal, wallows in mud to cool its body because it lacks sufficient sweat glands to regulate temperature.
The Baguio Panagbenga festival celebrates the seasonal blooming of local flora, featuring giant floats decorated with thousands of real pine needles and fresh vascular plant blossoms.
The bangus, or milkfish, is the national fish and survives in both saltwater and freshwater by specially adapting its gills to balance internal salts.
The tamaraw, an endangered buffalo endemic to Mindoro, has distinct V-shaped horns and prefers living in high-altitude montane forests and grassy clearings.
